question: How does the number and size of required B-I fire extinguishers generally change as a recreational vessel's length increases?
choice_a: The requirement decreases as vessel length increases
choice_b: It is fixed at exactly one extinguisher regardless of length
choice_c: Larger vessels must carry a greater number of extinguishers, or fewer larger-capacity B-II extinguishers, than smaller vessels with the same type of engine compartment
choice_d: Only vessels longer than 65 feet require any extinguisher
explanation: The minimum number and rating of required portable fire extinguishers scales up as vessel length increases, since larger vessels have more fuel and engine-compartment volume and greater potential fire risk.
source_note: Universal USCG fire-extinguisher carriage requirements by vessel length (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: When might a recreational vessel with an outboard engine and no enclosed fuel or engine compartment NOT be required to carry a fire extinguisher?
choice_a: A fire extinguisher is required on every vessel with an outboard engine regardless of configuration
choice_b: If it is built so that it cannot trap explosive or flammable gases or vapors, and it is not carrying flammable or combustible materials in quantity
choice_c: Whenever the vessel is operated on the Chesapeake Bay
choice_d: Only if the vessel is longer than 40 feet
explanation: Certain small open outboard boats without enclosed compartments where vapors could accumulate, and not carrying flammable materials, are exempt from the fire extinguisher carriage requirement under federal rules.
source_note: Universal USCG fire-extinguisher exemption for certain open outboard vessels (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: Which vessels may be exempt from carrying daytime visual distress signals, even though a nighttime signal is still generally required if operating after dark?
choice_a: Certain small, manually propelled or open Class A (under 16 ft) vessels operating during the day on certain waters, per federal VDS exemptions
choice_b: No vessel is ever exempt from VDS requirements
explanation: Federal rules exempt certain smaller, manually propelled, or specified open vessels from carrying daytime visual distress signals, though most of these same vessels still need a night signal if operated after dark.
source_note: Universal USCG visual distress signal daytime exemptions (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What is the practical difference between a B-I and a B-II rated fire extinguisher aboard a boat?
choice_a: A B-II extinguisher has a larger fire-suppression capacity than a B-I, so fewer B-II units (or a combination) can satisfy the requirement on larger vessels
choice_b: A B-I extinguisher only works on wood fires
choice_c: There is no difference; the labels are interchangeable
choice_d: A B-II extinguisher is used exclusively for electrical fires
explanation: B-II extinguishers carry a larger flammable-liquid fire-suppression rating than B-I units, so a vessel can sometimes satisfy its requirement with fewer, larger B-II extinguishers instead of multiple smaller B-I units.
source_note: Universal USCG fire-extinguisher rating classification (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What must a vessel less than 12 meters (about 39.4 feet) long carry to comply with sound-signaling requirements, if it does not have a mounted horn?
choice_a: Nothing; vessels under 12 meters have no sound-signal requirement
choice_b: Some other means of making an efficient sound signal, such as a whistle or air horn, audible at an appropriate distance
choice_d: A siren identical to law enforcement vessels
explanation: Vessels under 12 meters must carry at least an efficient sound-producing device, such as a whistle or handheld air horn, even if they do not have a fixed, mounted horn system.
source_note: Universal USCG/Navigation Rules sound-signaling equipment requirements by vessel length (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: For a boater planning an extended trip on the more open or remote stretches of the Chesapeake Bay, what additional emergency device is commonly recommended beyond standard VDS and a VHF radio?
choice_a: A personal locator beacon (PLB) or emergency position-indicating radio beacon (EPIRB), which can transmit a distress signal with GPS location to search-and-rescue authorities
choice_b: A second anchor with no additional communication device
choice_d: No additional device is ever recommended
explanation: A PLB or EPIRB can transmit a distress signal with the vessel's or person's GPS location directly to search-and-rescue authorities, providing an added layer of safety beyond VDS and VHF radio for longer or more remote trips.
source_note: Universal USCG emergency locator beacon guidance for recreational boaters (NASBLA-aligned course content)
